newsitem.title: USA: Florida Lt. Gov. to lead Miami oversight panel.
newsitem.headline: Florida Lt. Gov. to lead Miami oversight panel.

text.p: Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles appointed Lt. Gov. Kenneth "Buddy" MacKay and four longtime Miami business and government officials Monday to oversee the city's budget repair.
MacKay, who acted as Chiles' point man on the Hurricane Andrew recovery and the 1994 Summit of the Americas, will head the five-member oversight committee.
He stressed that the panel's role would be advisory and that city commissioners would still have to come up with their own solution to close Miami's $68 million budget deficit.
"We don't see ourselves as trying to run the city of Miami," MacKay said. "This is not something where you have to have parental guidance."
The lieutenant governor also said that bankruptcy was not a viable option for the city, which has spent more than it raised for years.

"Regardless of what got Miami into this, there's no excuse now for all of us not to work together to to get over this," MacKay said. "Miami can be restored. Miami should be restored and we're here to make sure it is restored."
Also appointed to the oversight panel were:
-- Robert Beatty, who has been BellSouth Telecommunications' general counsel in Miami since 1988. He is also chairman of the Beacon Council economic development organization.

-- Cynthia Curry, who is vice president of Florida International University and heads the school's business and finance division. She is the former assistant county manager for Dade County, Miami's county.
-- Adolfo Henriques, president of NationsBank Miami and manager of the bank's private client group.
-- Maria Camilla Leiva, the executive vice president of the Miami Free Zone Corp. She is a member of the Board of Directors for the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.

The panel was scheduled to hold its first meeting with city officials Tuesday. Chiles said he had not dictated a timetable for the panel, but added, "We all know the date you've heard is March is when you start running out of cash."

Miami Mayor Joe Carollo acknowledged that, "yes it is embarrassing" to have the city placed under state oversight. But he said he would unveil proposals at a Thursday city commission meeting for closing the budget gap without raising property taxes or doubling garbage fees.

He said that would require finding $50 million to $60 million in new, recurring revenues. Carollo was not specific but suggested the plan could include renegotiating leases and selling some city land, possibly a valuable waterfront parcel assessed at $125 million.
"This is a very real deficit, but we're far from being bankrupt," Carollo said. "We own over $1 billion of assets."
